categories.A: State origin. Text authored or commissioned by a Chinese state entity and published without substantive editorial alteration, whatever its topic. State media, government, party and diplomatic bodies, state-owned enterprises and the Hong Kong and Macao governments and statutory bodies are state entities; a press release from any other issuer is not state origin, even when it is published unaltered.
categories.B: Unchecked state sourcing. Written by the local outlet, and its central content is a factual claim attributed to a Chinese official or state source (an assertion of fact about events, numbers or actions), passed on without independent confirmation. A stated position, policy, warning, threat, opinion or denial is not a factual claim, and reporting one is independent journalism even without outside comment.
categories.C: Independent journalism. The outlet's own reporting, including reporting that quotes Chinese officials but confirms, contextualizes or contests what they say, and reporting of a position, policy, warning, threat, opinion or denial attributed to a Chinese official or state source, with or without outside comment. A press release that is not state origin is counted here when it substantively concerns China.
categories.not_relevant: Does not concern China in any substantive way. A Hong Kong, Macao or Taiwan domestic story counts as China coverage only when it substantively concerns the PRC state or its policy.

distribution_wires.note: Global press release distribution services. Their releases are written by their issuers and pushed worldwide, so they are counted as the worldwide distribution stratum (WLD in latest.json), never attributed to the United States and never added into any country.

language_editions.note: Language editions of one release on a distribution wire are one underlying item; each edition is its own page and stays a placement.

numbered_series.note: The numbered parts, (1) to (n), of one story at one outlet on one day (an Italpress photo story, a Europa Press release split into parts) count as one placement.

same_page.note: One page stored at two addresses (Adnkronos Immediapress, with and without the distributor in the path) counts once.

alteration.label: Alteration score
alteration.method_text:
The alteration score tests the second half of the state origin definition, that the text is reproduced without substantive editorial alteration. It sets each state origin copy beside the earliest version of the same text that can be found: the state outlet's own page (a reference original) where one is found, otherwise an earlier copy of the same item at another monitored outlet. Only a reference original is the state text itself; against an earlier monitored copy the score says how far one outlet's copy differs from another's, and every figure says which kind of original it rests on. It is report only: it never changes a label, a count or a denominator, and a copy with a high score keeps its label. At the last export 195 of 2272 state origin copies had an original (39 from a reference source, 156 an earlier monitored copy), and 2 had both texts available to score: 0 against a reference original and 2 against an earlier monitored copy, from 2 distinct originals and 2 distinct underlying items. No copy has yet been scored against the state outlet's own text, so every score so far measures change against an earlier monitored copy, not against the state original.

An original is looked for first among the reference sources, the English and other editions of Chinese state outlets read only as originals. A reference item qualifies when the copy's credit names its publisher, it is in the copy's language, it appeared from eleven days before the copy to one day after it, and its headline, feed summary or body fingerprint nearly repeats the copy's; when both texts are available at least 30 percent of the copy's words must line up with it. Failing that, the original is the earliest credited copy of the same item at another monitored outlet, in the same language, outside the copy's own media group: sister papers of one group (the ACM regional mastheads, the Postmedia papers, the Nine or News Corp mastheads) share one copy pool, so a sister's earlier copy is the same placement, not an original. Translations are never matched across languages, so an Italian copy of Xinhua English has no reference original and is counted as a translation. Copies first seen in the last 14 days are paired again at every export.

Both texts are compared after credit lines, datelines and lines an outlet repeats on many of its pages are removed. The score is the share of the copy's words that are not found in the original, in runs of three words or more. Cuts are reported separately as the share of the original kept, and headline changes as a headline similarity. The provisional bands are verbatim (under 3 percent new words), light (under 15 percent), moderate (under 40 percent) and substantial (40 percent or more). Many copies repeat one original, so the shares in the lead count each underlying item once, with the number of copies beside them, and an outlet is ranked, or a median given, only from 5 distinct originals.

The bands measure wording, not meaning. A copy can keep every word and still change the sense by cutting a paragraph, and a copy can score as substantial because an outlet added its own background or a rebuttal. Two keyword cues, one for local context and one for counterpoint, flag added text for a reader to check; they are weak and never a finding on their own. Bodies are stored only where the tracker runs, so only copies whose two texts are both available are scored, and the coverage line says how many that is; each reference source's counts of pages fetched, expired, failed and paywalled are given beside it. Every copy in the substantial band is listed for review by hand, and a blind hand check of 20 pairs per band tests both the pairs and the bands.

doctrine.label: Doctrine terms
doctrine.method_text:
The doctrine term tracker counts how often China coverage uses the Chinese state's own set phrases, such as community with a shared future, true multilateralism, Chinese modernization and the one-China principle. There are 13 families of terms. Each family is matched in English and in the renderings Chinese state media and the Chinese foreign ministry publish in the outlet's language; a language is left out of a family when no such rendering was found, or when the rendering is ordinary prose in that language, and every language is also matched on the English terms. The terms are read in the headline, the feed summary and the whole body, and every occurrence is counted, though an acronym in brackets beside its full term is the same mention and counts once with it. A match is a keyword match, not a reading of the article: it says the phrase is there, not who used it or whether the article endorses it.

Some matches are excluded by rule. A bare win-win is ordinary English and never counts, only win-win cooperation; hegemonism counts but the generic hegemony does not; the one-China principle is kept apart from the one China policy other governments state. An acronym counts only when a full term of the same family appears in the same article, and GSI only beside Global Security Initiative itself, so BRI in Indonesian football or banking news is not the Belt and Road. Belt and Road, Multipolar world, Global South and People-to-people exchanges are common well beyond Chinese state usage, so they are shown muted and left out of the share of articles using the vocabulary. Multipolar world and People-to-people exchanges are also the stated policy of other governments, India, Russia, Vietnam and the BRICS among them, so they are counted only when a China word (China, Chinese, Beijing, Xi Jinping and their renderings in the article's language) appears within 140 characters of the phrase.

Rates are per 1,000 China articles of each kind (state origin, unchecked state sourcing, independent journalism) on the same days, counting only articles already tagged under the current term list. Where a body has not been read the headline and summary alone are matched, which finds fewer phrases; the article is tagged again once its body arrives. A hand check codes up to 200 matches, spread evenly over the families first and over each family's languages within it, each shown with about 30 words either side, stored when the article is tagged so the sample does not depend on where it is drawn. A family is checked at a precision of at least 0.9 on at least 15 coded matches and withheld below 0.8 once 5 are coded, and a withheld family shows no figure; the measure as a whole is checked when the matches of the families still shown reach 0.9 together.

speed.label: Republication speed
speed.method_text:
Republication speed is the time between a state original and a state origin copy of it in a monitored outlet. It is measured only for copies paired with their original (see the alteration score), and only when both publication times are credible: readable, not after the item was discovered, and not before collection began. The time the tracker discovered an item is never used as a lag. Where the original is the state outlet's own page, collected as a reference source, the lag is absolute. Where no such page was found and the original is the first monitored copy, the lag is relative, behind the first monitored copy, and the two are never pooled. Lags fall into four buckets: the same hour, the same day (1 to 24 hours), 1 to 3 days, and later. A copy up to an hour ahead of its original counts as the same hour, since clocks differ by minutes. When either page gives only a date, the pair is bucketed by calendar date instead (same date, 1 to 3 days, later) and kept out of the medians. The days are counted in one zone, the zone of the date: the state outlets' dates are Beijing dates (the Global Times sitemap's are UTC dates), and the other page's time is converted into that zone before the days are counted. Copies more than an hour ahead of their original, and pairs without a credible time, are counted but kept outside every distribution. One state text run by many outlets of one group is many pairs but one original, so every figure gives the distinct originals beside the pairs, and a median needs distinct originals, not pairs: an outlet gets a median from 10 timed pairs with 10 distinct originals; a route, country or source from 5. An earlier copy at a sister outlet of the same media group is never the first monitored copy. Wires are counted under WLD. At the last export, 37 absolute pairs fell inside the distributions, with 26 distinct originals.

The times are what the pages say, and they are not always what they seem. Many sites give the time a page was last updated as its publication time: on the copy that makes it look slower than it was, and on the original it can put a copy ahead of its source. Some state listings label their time zones wrongly: a Beijing time written as UTC reads eight hours late. Times are corrected per source when they are collected, and the export checks every reference source for this by comparing publication with discovery: the median gap, the share published after it was discovered, and the share that give only a date, overall and among items more than a day old, by when the page's own time should have been read. Discovery can only show a time that reads late. A time that reads early is caught where a source lists an item twice: CGTN's sitemap writes Beijing time marked as UTC, so its times are read as Beijing time, and every item it shares with CGTN's RSS feed is compared; if CGTN began writing true UTC, the sitemap would read eight hours earlier than the feed and the source would be flagged. Each source's counts of pages fetched, expired, failed and paywalled are given beside it. Pages that give only a date can say no more than the calendar day. State text also reaches outlets by channels the tracker cannot see, such as wire terminals, email and agreements, so a lag is the time between two public pages, not the time it took the text to travel. Coverage is partial: only copies paired with an original count, the reference sources reach back only a few days, and most copies have no original found. The hand check compares the bucket of 60 reference pairs, read by a person from the times shown on both pages, with the measure's bucket, and passes at 85 percent agreement.

spikes.label: Unusual days
spikes.method_text:
Unusual days are days on which a country, or the worldwide press release wires, carried far more state origin text than usual. What is counted is the day's distinct underlying items, each outlet adding at most 3 of them, so one outlet's batch or one item placed many times is a lump and never a surge on its own. Each complete day is compared with the 28 complete days before it, counting only the days on which the country's outlets were collected at all, and at least 14 of them are needed. The expected count is the mean of those days after the busiest tenth of them is set aside, and never less than 0.2. Daily counts vary more than chance alone would make them, so the spread is taken from the country's own last 90 days (a negative binomial model). A day is flagged when it counts at least 5, at least three times the expected count, with a chance under 1 in 1,000 of reaching that count on an ordinary day. The day the export runs is partial and is never tested. China is not monitored and has no series. Over the 7,342 country days tested so far, 1 was flagged. The model puts the number it would flag by chance alone at about 0.2, but it assumes each country's days vary as they did before, and real days are lumpier, so that figure is a rough guide and not a promise.

Each flagged day lists the outlets and underlying items behind it, and the checks that could make it an artefact of the instrument rather than a surge of state text: a newly added outlet, a backfill read, a collector recovering from an outage, an incomplete day for the collector on the owner's machine, a ruleset or relevance gate change, saturated feeds on the baseline days, the daily model cap, and a surge in everything discovered rather than in state text alone. A day with any of these is shown muted with its reason, as one to check, and a day with none is shown as clean. A ruleset change counts only when it took effect inside the 28 days a day is compared with and the labels on the two sides still differ in age: until the older days are labelled again under the new rules, those days stay to check, and the site says so; a change stops affecting new days 28 days after it. The repeats in the discovery counts before they were fixed are noted too, but they touch only the rate per discovered item, not the count. Unusual days are report only: they change no count, and a hand check of up to 30 flagged days, each judged a real surge or an artefact, has to find at least 80 percent real before the marking provisional comes off.

relay_provisional_reason: No hand coding study has reported yet. The sample drawn on 12 October 2026 was set aside before coding began: every one of its 1,400 labels was made under a classifier prompt older than the current one (786 by the API and 614 in a session, none carrying a prompt tag), so a study on it would check labels that are being replaced. A new sample is drawn from labels made under the current classifier prompt (2026-10-17) once the runner has relabelled them, and the study compares the coders with those labels. The counts stay provisional until the owner and two research assistants have hand coded a fixed random sample, about 200 articles in each language with at least 300 model labelled articles, stratified by language and, within each language, by the model's current category, and Cohen's kappa between their codes and the model's on unchecked state sourcing versus independent journalism is at least 0.6, with the coders and the model each placing at least 10 articles in unchecked state sourcing, overall and in every language with enough items. A study in which the model finds unchecked state sourcing at least 10 times and the coders fewer has failed.

relay_reliability_history.note: A stability check, not a basis for publication: the same model judged the same articles twice, with the same prompt, which detects randomness in its own judgement and nothing about a bias it holds every time.
